title: Developmental bias explains the evolutionary trend towards simple leaf shapes
abstract: The relative influence of developmental bias and natural selection on evolutionary outcomes remains a central, unresolved question in evolutionary biology. Here, we combine large-scale phylogenetic trees with herbarium data to confirm that, across the evolutionary history of angiosperms, transitions from complex to simple leaf shapes have occurred at a significantly higher rate than the reverse. To investigate whether this directional trend reflects an underlying developmental bias, we simulate evolutionary transitions by introducing random mutations into a well-established computational model of leaf development. Despite excluding selection, the transition rates produced by the model closely align with those observed in the phylogenetic data. abstract: Multidrug-resistant fungal pathogens are a serious threat to public health and global food security. Mitigation requires the discovery of antifungal compounds with novel modes of action along with a comprehensive understanding of the molecular mechanisms governing antifungal resistance. title: A kinetic error filtering mechanism for enzyme-free copying of nucleic acid sequences
abstract: Accurate copying of nucleic acid sequences is essential for self-replicating systems. Modern cells achieve error ratios as low as 10−9 with sophisticated enzymes capable of kinetic proofreading. In contrast, experiments probing enzyme-free copying of RNA and DNA as potential prebiotic replication processes find error ratios on the order of 10%. Given this low intrinsic copying fidelity, plausible scenarios for the spontaneous emergence of molecular evolution require an accuracy-enhancing mechanism. Here, we study a 'kinetic error filtering' scenario that dramatically boosts the likelihood of producing exact copies of nucleic acid sequences. title: Ramping-up hippocampal ripples and their neocortical coupling support human visual short-term memory
abstract: Emerging evidence suggests that the hippocampus contributes to visual short-term memory (VSTM). However, the neural mechanisms through which hippocampal activity supports the maintenance of VSTM representations remain largely unknown. Here, using intracranial EEG recordings from human participants performing a delayed match-to-sample task for naturalistic objects, we investigated the role of hippocampal ripple activity—brief high-frequency oscillations associated with memory replay—in VSTM maintenance and hippocampal-neocortical communication. We found that hippocampal ripple rates progressively ramped up during the maintenance period and supported successful VSTM. abstract: A much-replicated finding in human brain imaging is a distributed ‘multiple-demand’ or MD system, increasing in activity for many kinds of cognitive demand, and centrally involved in cognitive control. title: Blood-derived dietary protein promotes sleep in the mosquito Aedes aegypti
abstract: Sleep is a ubiquitous, yet highly variable, behavior across species. The duration and timing of sleep are influenced by ecological demands and dietary context. In the mosquito Aedes aegypti, a blood-feeding insect with specialized nutritional requirements, the relationship between feeding and sleep remains poorly understood. Here, we investigated how blood-derived dietary protein influences sleep regulation. title: Rethinking laboratory sustainability
abstract: Green lab initiatives like My Green Lab and LEAF (Laboratory Efficiency Assessment Framework), are paving the way towards sustainable research by promoting resource efficiency, energy conservation, and waste reduction through behavioral changes. However, these initiatives focus almost exclusively on material consumption, overlooking deeper facets of scientific waste that stem from questionable research practices: the environmental cost of unnecessary or poorly designed experiments, discarded null results, unreproducible research, and distorted reporting. abstract: Lumen formation is a key process during the morphogenesis of tubular organs, such as the vertebrate vascular network. abstract: Chromatin is dynamic at all length scales, influencing chromatin-based processes, such as gene expression. abstract: This study reveals an unrecognized mechanism by which platelets retract and compact fibrin fibers. abstract: Diurnal rhythms influence insect behavior, physiology, and metabolism, optimizing their performance by adapting to daily changes in the environment. Nature Communications, Published online: 24 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41467-026-79701-4

Plant-fungal interactions in the rhizosphere influence plant health. Here the authors describe an optically transparent granular microgel matrix that mimics the mechanical properties of natural microenvironments to dissect fungal development and pathogenesis.

title: Bacteria-induced TLR2 signaling unleashes multiple mechanisms to reduce Treg immunosuppression and enhance cancer immunity
abstract:
Nature Communications, Published online: 24 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41467-026-79362-3

Toll-like receptor (TLR) signaling is known to support T cell priming, but how different TLRs regulate intratumoral effector T cell function is unknown. The authors here demonstrate that TLR2 signaling in dendritic cells upon Listeria infection enhances cancer immunity by disrupting regulatory T cells and promoting tumor antigen presentation by DCs to CD8 T cells.

title: Promoted phase transition in perovskite heterojunctions via in-situ regulated 2D intermediates enables stable solar cells
abstract:
Nature Communications, Published online: 24 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41467-026-79294-y

Efficient perovskite solar cells require graded layered junctions, yet spacer-driven ion exchange offers poor control. Yue et al. added a preformed layered perovskite to direct vertical phase growth at the buried interface, improving efficiency, stability, and module scalability.

title: Iso-Seq enables discovery of novel isoform variants in human retina at single-cell resolution
abstract:
Nature Communications, Published online: 24 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41467-026-78606-6

Iso-Seq enabled isoform discovery of human retina at single cell levels. This study revealed novel isoforms, splice junctions and alternative promoters across major retinal cell types, providing insights into the retinal transcriptomic landscape.

title: Single-molecule landscape of DNA replication pausing
abstract:
Nature Communications, Published online: 24 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41467-026-79296-w

Rare DNA replication pauses can destabilise genomes but are hard to detect. Here, the authors use single-molecule nanopore sequencing to map pauses across a eukaryotic genome. They find widespread pauses enriched near transcribed genes and with a leading-strand bias over the promoter of an epigenetically regulated gene.

title: Rethinking Klebsiella pneumoniae vaccines: from protective immunity to rational vaccine design
abstract:
Nature Communications, Published online: 24 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41467-026-79574-7

This Review highlights barriers to cross-protective Klebsiella pneumoniae vaccines and proposes a paradigm shift, integrating antigen discovery, systems immunology and translational models to define conserved protective targets and immune correlates.

title: Global intercomparison of ocean-based geochemical carbon dioxide removal efficiencies
abstract:

The study presents a unified framework for ocean CO₂ removal efficiencies, maps global direct ocean removal efficiency, and combines it with ocean alkalinity enhancement simulations to estimate CO2 outgassing from weathering products in the ocean.

abstract:

There are compelling reasons to expect polygenic adaptation to be common, yet direct evidence is lacking. Conversely, there are hundreds of examples of large-effect adaptations across species, but it is unclear whether they occur frequently within any given species. These different lines of evidence are hard to synthesize, in part due to the lack of theory that relates them.
